Posted December 17, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Once again the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has caused a major headache for the prohibitionists. This new case is ANGEL MCCLARY RAICH; DIANE MONSON; JOHN DOE, Number One; JOHN DOE, Number Two, Versus ASHCROFT.
(Angel Raich is the wife [not the daughter, as some articles reported] of my good friend Robert Raich, the attorney for the Oakland CBC. Diane Monson is a patient whose six plants were destroyed by DEA agents, and the John Does are growers for Angel.)

Their suit sought to enjoin the feds from depriving them of their medical cannabis, and arresting them or Angel's growers. A lower court had declined to enjoin the feds, but now the Court of Appeals has told it to reconsider.

The key practical point here is that no money changes hands, so there is no commerce. Although this ruling technically applies only to these four individuals, in reality any person in the 9th Circuit who is similarly situated will also be protected. In the real world, the feds do not have the resources to go after most patients who have their own gardens, so the number of people directly affected may be limited. On the other hand, patients can certainly feel more secure, and state officials who try to use the federal law as an excuse for ignoring their states medical cannabis laws will have to find another excuse for their predations at least for the time being.

This ruling is similar to what happened in the Oakland CBC case. In September of 1999, a panel of judges on the 9th Circuit ruled in favor of the Oakland CBC, saying that a patient's narrowly defined medical necessity could override the federal prohibition against distributing medical cannabis.
See
Federal Appeals Court Opens Door For Medical Marijuana Clubs
NORML Weekly Press Release
and
Ninth Circuit Ruling On Oakland Case -- Full Text

Unfortunately, but predictably, the feds appealed and got a stay of the ruling that protected the clubs. It is not clear that the feds will be able to get a stay that would interfere with the rights of individual patients the way they stopped the clubs as they did in August of 2000.
See
Supreme Court Grants Emergency Stay Against Oakland CBC. Arbitrary Power Trumps Basic Rights.

At the time, I pointed out that the majority of the Court went even further and suggested that the medical defense would not even be available to individual users of medical cannabis. This bit of judicial overreach is called dicta. (Dicta are defined " as a judge's expressions of opinion on a point other than the precise issue involved in determining a case. " )

This suggestion provoked three of the Justices to issue a " concurring " opinion in which they agree that medical necessity does not apply to the distributors, so the marijuana will have to come like manna from heaven, but they still insist that the patients have a right to manna.

The good news was that the conservative majority did leave open the possibility of a States Rights argument and the Raich/Monson case was a response to that invitation.

Justice Stevens, wrote a concurring opinion with Justice Souter and Justice Ginsburg joining him in which they responded to the dicta:
Apart from its limited holding, the Court takes two unwarranted and unfortunate excursions that prevent me from joining its opinion. Second, the Court gratuitously casts doubt on " whether necessity can ever be a defense " to any federal statute that does not explicitly provide for it, calling such a defense into question by a misleading reference to its existence as an " open question. " Ante, at 5, 6. By contrast, our precedent has expressed no doubt about the viability of the common-law defense, even in the context of federal criminal statutes that do not provide for it in so many words.

Indeed, the Court's comment on the general availability of the necessity defense is completely unnecessary because the Government has made no such suggestion...

The Court's opinion on this point is pure dictum.

The overbroad language of the Court's opinion is especially unfortunate given the importance of showing respect for the sovereign States that comprise our Federal Union. That respect imposes a duty on federal courts, whenever possible, to avoid or minimize conflict between federal and state law, particularly in situations in which the citizens of a State have chosen to " serve as a laboratory " in the trial of " novel social and economic experiments without risk to the rest of the country "

In my view, this is such a case. By passing Proposition 215, California voters have decided that seriously ill patients and their primary caregivers should be exempt from prosecution under state laws for cultivating and possessing marijuana if the patient's physician recommends using the drug for treatment. This case does not call upon the Court to deprive all such patients of the benefit of the necessity defense to federal prosecution, when the case itself does not involve any such patients

Obviously, the dicta proffered by the five Justices in the Oakland CBC case does not make one optimistic about their ruling in our favor in this case, but there is at least a chance that they will do so.

Notably, the five did say, Finally, we share Justice Stevens concern for showing respect for the sovereign States that comprise our Federal Union. Nor are we passing today on a constitutional question, such as whether the Controlled Substances Act exceeds Congress power under the Commerce Clause.

The point about the Commerce Clause was raised in the Raich case by dissenting judge, C. Arlen Beam, a visiting judge from the federal appeals court in St. Louis, who said marijuana was a commercial product under the broad definition used by Congress and upheld by the Supreme Court.

The cultivation of marijuana for medicinal purposes is commercial in nature. The argument ignores the fungible, economic nature of the substance at issue marijuana plants for which there is a well-established and variable interstate market, albeit an illegal one under federal law.

He cited a 1942 case in which grain grown by a farmer for his own family's use was ruled to be subject to the Interstate Commerce clause. Of course, the federal government was and is directly involved in the agricultural markets, but only indirectly involved in the cannabis markets through prohibition.

The conservative majority on the Supreme Court is strongly in favor of States Rights, and if there is any immediate cause for optimism, it could be found in the Court's recent refusal even to hear the Drug Czar's attempt to deprive doctors of the right to recommend medical cannabis to their patients, thereby upholding another 9th Circuit ruling.
See
Federal Judge Stops Drug Czar's Threat To Pull Licenses of Doctors Who Recommend Medical Marijuana.

A victory for the patients at the Supreme Court would be devastating to the prohibitionists, but ultimately, even if we lose, this case makes clear that the federal government is doing something that an overwhelming majority of the American people strongly oppose.
